title: Does Giving a Great Deal Entitle You to Something in Return?
deck: Giving may ask to be acknowledged, but cannot unilaterally sign another person up to future obligations.
body: Giving within a relationship is rarely entirely without expectation.

We spend time keeping someone company, give up our own arrangements, offer resources when the other person is in difficulty, and adjust our lives in many unseen ways. Even if we never say it, we may hope that when we need them, they will stand beside us in the same way.
There is nothing base about this expectation.
If one person bears the burden for a long time while the other only receives, the giver will grow tired and begin to wonder whether they are being taken seriously.
But expecting something in return is not the same as already being entitled to it.
After giving, someone can easily begin to keep an account in their mind.

I did these things for you, so now you should agree to my request; I once gave up an opportunity, so you should give one up too; I stayed when things were hardest for you, so you must not leave me in the future.
This account may be entirely real, but it may never have been visible to both people.

The person accepting help knows what they received, but may not know what conditions the helper has simultaneously written into the future. Only when those conditions are finally raised do they discover that every past act of goodwill may be a belated contract.
The problem is not that relationships cannot involve exchange.

Living together inherently requires commitments, a division of work, and mutual responsibility. Two people can explicitly agree: I will carry more for this period, and afterward you will need to take over; I am willing to support this choice, but we must share certain risks.
Such an agreement is different because both people have a chance to know the conditions and to refuse or revise them.
Unilateral giving, however, cannot automatically create obligations the other person never accepted.
I can decide to give my time, but that decision alone cannot decide for you how you must repay it in the future.
This does not mean the recipient may take every contribution for granted.

Responses within a relationship do not arise only from explicit contracts. Long-standing trust, real reliance, and commitments already made also create responsibilities. If someone knows the other person keeps bearing burdens for them, yet never asks about the cost and is unwilling to respond within their capacity, it is hard to say they have no responsibility at all.
But responsibility needs to be explained, not calculated directly from the total amount given.

Some contributions were requested; others were the helper’s own initiative. Some really solved the recipient’s problems; others mainly met the helper’s need to feel they “must be useful.” Putting them all in the same ledger conceals their differences.
Especially in intimate relationships, giving is often treated as a way of gaining control of someone’s direction.
“I’ve done so much for you, so I know best what matters to you.”
“I have carried the most, so in the end you should listen to me.”
Here giving no longer asks only for a fair response. It also asks another person to surrender their place as the one who decides.
But carrying more does not automatically make someone more entitled to decide who another person should become.

If a choice will continue to use shared resources, the giver certainly has a stronger say and may refuse to keep contributing. But what they control is their own resources and manner of participation, not the whole of another person’s life.
They can say:
“I can no longer support you in the same way.”
But having offered support in the past does not by itself entitle them to say:
“So you must live in the direction I choose.”
Sometimes the most honest relationship is not one that pretends there are no expectations, but one that expresses them earlier.
“I am willing to do this, but over the long term I will need a response from you.”
“I can bear this on this occasion, but it cannot become a permanent arrangement.”
These words may be less moving than unconditional giving, but they give the other person a chance to participate genuinely.
Unspoken conditions often turn into accusations through disappointment. Making conditions clear lets both people know what they are building together.
Having given a great deal can certainly be a reason for a conversation.
It can show that the relationship has become unbalanced, justify asking for responsibilities to be redistributed, and give someone grounds to stop giving.
But giving itself cannot sign the other person up to an unlimited obligation to repay.
Real reciprocity is not two people finally balancing every entry in the account.
It is both people seeing what each has borne and being willing to let those facts affect their choices, without turning past giving into ownership of another person’s future.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
